title: My body: its parts, the bones inside and the muscles that move them
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 1 Biology, Unit 3.3 'Our bodies' (naming the main parts of the body), and goes further into bones, joints, muscles and skin. No textbook needed.
summary: Your child learns the real names of the parts of their body, finds that most come in pairs and that each one has a job, and then discovers what is hidden inside: a skeleton of bones, joints where it bends, and muscles that pull the bones, like the strings of a puppet. They trace a life-size picture of themselves, try five jobs without thumbs, try to eat with a stiff elbow, and find out that a newborn baby has more bones than a grown-up.
builds_on: This is the first rung. In Class 4 your child comes back to the skeleton: the four jobs of bones, muscles working in pairs, and animals with backbones, shells and no bones at all. In Class 5 they go inside the body to the organs: heart, lungs, stomach, kidneys and brain.
subconcepts: naming the main parts of the body
left and right: body parts that come in pairs
every body part has a job
the thumb that can touch every finger
bones and the skeleton inside us
joints: the places where we bend
muscles pull bones to move us
skin: the covering that keeps us in and feels the world
a baby has more bones than a grown-up
every body is different, and every body is a human body
one body made of trillions of cells, with about as many microbes living on and in it
homeostasis: the body keeps itself just right (sweating, shivering, thirst)
other animals have the same parts used for different jobs
looking after our body: moving, resting, washing
goals: By the end your child can point to and name at least 15 parts of the body, including elbow, wrist, shoulder, hip, knee, ankle and heel.
By the end your child can say which body parts come in pairs and which come one at a time.
By the end your child can say what a bone is, what a joint is and what a muscle does, and feel each on their own body.
By the end your child can explain, from their own test, why a thumb or an elbow matters.
By the end your child can say that a bird's wing, a whale's flipper and their own arm are built from the same kinds of bones.
By the end your child can say that bodies are all different and all work in the same way.
words: joint
a place where two bones meet and the body can bend, like the elbow or knee
bone
a hard, strong, living part inside the body that holds it up
skeleton
all the bones of the body together
muscle
the soft, strong part under the skin that pulls on bones to move them
skin
the stretchy covering of the whole body that keeps germs out and feels touch
skull
the hard bony box that keeps the brain safe
ribs
the curved bones round the chest that guard the heart and lungs
spine
the backbone: a chain of small bones down the middle of the back
thumb
the short, strong finger that can touch every other finger
pair
two of the same kind, like two eyes or two ears

days.title: Life-size me
days.goal: Name the parts of the body on a life-size picture of your child.

steps.title: Touch and say
steps.do: Play 'Touch and say'. Call out a body part and your child touches it on their own body as fast as they can: head, nose, chin, neck, shoulder, elbow, wrist, tummy, hip, knee, ankle, heel, toes. Then swap: your child calls and you touch, and make one deliberate mistake (touch your knee for 'elbow') to see if they catch you. Ask: 'Which part did you not know the name of?' Most children have never been told the names wrist, ankle, heel or hip; say them clearly.

steps.title: Trace yourself
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Your child lies on a big sheet of paper (or old newspaper sheets taped together) on the floor while you draw round them with a crayon. Together, write labels with arrows: head, neck, shoulder, chest, tummy, arm, elbow, wrist, hand, fingers, thumb, hip, leg, knee, ankle, foot, heel, toes. Ask your child to say each word as they write or stick it. If they cannot write yet, you write and they point.

steps.title: Two of these, one of those
steps.do: Look at the picture together. Ask: 'Which parts do you have two of?' (eyes, ears, arms, hands, legs, feet, knees, elbows, shoulders, nostrils). 'Which do you have only one of?' (nose, mouth, head, neck, tummy, belly button). Fold the picture down the middle along the nose and tummy: 'Is the left side the same as the right?' Nearly. Say: 'Our bodies come in a left half and a right half, almost like a mirror. Scientists call that symmetry.'

need: a big sheet of paper or old newspapers taped together

days.title: Every part has a job
days.goal: Find out, by losing it for a morning, what the thumb does, and give each body part a job.

steps.title: Thumb check
steps.do: Ask your child to touch the tip of the thumb to the tip of each finger in turn, then try to touch the tip of the little finger to each other finger. 'Which one can reach all the others?' Only the thumb. Say: 'This thumb that can turn round to face your fingers is one of the most useful things a human body has.'

steps.title: A morning without thumbs
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Tape your child's thumbs gently against the side of their hands with soft cloth tape (or tie them with a soft hair band). First ask: 'Which job will be hardest without thumbs?' Then give them five jobs: do up a button, pick up five grains of rice, hold a pencil and write their name, open a water bottle, eat a piece of dosa or chapati. Ask after each: 'Easy, hard or impossible?' and record it with a tick, a wavy line or a cross. Take the tape off straight away if anything hurts.

steps.title: What does it do?
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1 together. Read each question aloud. For the matching section, act each one out first: 'Show me what your knee is for' (bending the leg to walk, sit, jump). Good answers name an action, not just a place.

need: soft cloth tape or soft hair bands
a shirt with buttons, rice grains, a pencil, a water bottle, a dosa or chapati

days.title: The hard parts inside
days.goal: Feel the bones under the skin and meet the skeleton.

steps.title: Bone hunt
steps.do: Ask your child to press gently all over themselves and find places where something hard is just under the skin: the knee cap, the elbow tip, the knuckles, the shin, the collarbone, the ribs, the skull at the top of the head, the jaw. Each time, say: 'That hard thing is a bone.' Ask: 'Is there bone in your ear? In the tip of your nose?' (No: those are bendy cartilage. Let them wobble it.)

steps.title: Read the story
steps.do: Read aloud 'Ponni and the Strings Inside' (the story in this rung). It is told by Ponni, a string puppet from Tamil Nadu. Read it slowly. Stop once, after Ponni asks where Kavya's strings are, and ask: 'Where do you think Kavya's strings are?' Accept any guess and carry on reading.

steps.title: Talk about the story
steps.do: Ask the story questions: 'How is Ponni's knee like Kavya's knee?' (both bend in one place, at a joint). 'What did Kavya feel in her arm when she lifted it?' (something hard, the bone, and something that went fat and hard, the muscle). 'Who pulls Kavya's strings?' (she does, from inside). Let your child feel their own upper arm while they bend the elbow.

steps.title: A skeleton inside
steps.do: Say: 'All your bones together are called your skeleton. A grown-up has 206 bones. More than half of them are in the hands and feet.' Hold up both hands: 'Each hand has 27 bones.' Ask: 'Why do you think hands need so many small bones?' (so they can bend in many places and do fiddly jobs).

days.title: Joints: where we bend
days.goal: Find out what joints do by stopping one, and sort the joints by how they move.

steps.title: Bend count
steps.do: Ask your child to bend every place on their body that bends, one at a time, saying the name: neck, shoulder, elbow, wrist, each finger joint, back, hip, knee, ankle, toes. Say: 'Every place you can bend is a joint, where two bones meet.' Count them together for one finger: how many bends? (three on a finger, two on the thumb).

steps.title: The stiff elbow
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Roll a newspaper into a tube and tape it loosely round your child's arm over the elbow so the arm stays straight. Put a biscuit on the table. Ask: 'Can you eat the biscuit with this hand?' Let them try. Then ask: 'How could you do it?' (bend at the shoulder and lean the head down, or get a friend to feed you). Take it off and try again. Ask: 'What does the elbow joint let you do?'

steps.title: Door joint, ball joint
steps.do: Open and close a door: 'The door swings one way on its hinge. Your elbow and knee are like that: they are hinge joints.' Now have your child swing the arm round in a big circle at the shoulder: 'Your shoulder can go round and round. It is a ball joint: a round end of bone sitting in a cup.' Show with your fist (the ball) inside your other cupped hand (the cup), turning it.

steps.title: Sushruta's 300 bones
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v1. Say: 'Long ago in India, a book of surgery named after the teacher Sushruta told doctors to learn the body by looking very carefully inside it, layer by layer. It counted about 300 bones. Doctors today count 206 in a grown-up.' Ask: 'Why might two careful people get different numbers?' (they counted different things: Sushruta's book counted teeth, nails and soft bendy cartilage as bones too).

days.title: Muscles: the strings inside
days.goal: Feel muscles pull on bones and build a card arm that moves when you pull a string.

steps.title: Feel the pull
steps.do: Your child puts one hand on the front of the other upper arm and slowly bends that elbow, bringing the hand up to the shoulder. Ask: 'What happened under your hand?' (it got fat and hard). Then straighten it: 'Now?' (soft again, and the back of the arm goes hard). Say: 'That is a muscle. Muscles can only pull, never push. So you need one to pull your arm up and another to pull it back down.'

steps.title: The card arm
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Cut two strips of card for the upper arm and lower arm, join them with a split pin as the elbow, and tape a string to the lower arm near the elbow. Thread it up through a loop of tape on the upper arm. Pull the string: the arm bends. Ask: 'Which part is the bone? Which is the joint? What is the string pretending to be?' (the muscle).

steps.title: Bone Builder board game
steps.do: Play the board game g1, 'Bone Builder'. Each square asks your child to move a joint, name a body part or answer a question. Play to the end once.

need: two strips of thin card, a split pin (paper fastener), string, tape, scissors (a grown-up cuts)
the printed board game, a die and a counter each

days.title: Skin, sameness and animals
days.goal: Look closely at skin, see that all bodies differ but share one plan, and find our bones in other animals.

steps.title: Skin detective
steps.do: Look at the skin on the back of your child's hand with a magnifying glass, or with your phone camera zoomed in. Ask: 'What can you see?' (lines, tiny hairs, little holes where sweat comes out). Press a fingertip on a clean mirror or steel plate, breathe on it, and look at the fingerprint. Say: 'Skin keeps germs out, keeps water in, and feels everything you touch. It is the biggest part of your body.'

steps.title: Every body is different
steps.do: Stand together in front of a mirror, or look at a family photo. Ask: 'How are our bodies different?' (height, skin colour, hair, size of hands, some people use a wheelchair or have one hand). 'How are they the same?' (same bones, same joints, all can feel, all need food and sleep). Tell your child about voice v2: 'A doctor called Vesalius found that the old books about the body were wrong in places, because the writer had cut open monkeys, not people. He said: look at real bodies yourself.' Ask: 'Why is it better to look than to just believe a book?'

steps.title: Bones in other animals
steps.do: Before the sheet, draw a quick arm: one bone from shoulder to elbow, two bones from elbow to wrist, then many small bones in the hand. Say: 'A bird's wing, a whale's flipper and a bat's wing have this same pattern of bones inside.' Then do Worksheet ws2 together.

steps.title: Foot and forearm
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. Measure your child's foot with string, then hold the string along their forearm from wrist crease to elbow crease. Do the same for everyone at home. Ask: 'Are they nearly the same? Is anyone different?' Say: 'Bodies grow in a pattern, but every body is a little different.'

steps.title: Looking after my body
steps.do: Ask: 'What does your body need from you every day?' Listen for: moving and playing, sleep, food and water, washing, being careful with the bones (helmets, not jumping from high walls). Write your child's three favourite answers on the life-size picture from Day 1.

need: a magnifying glass or a phone camera
a piece of string or wool

days.title: One and many, and just right
days.goal: Find out that one body is made of trillions of living cells and microbes, and that it keeps itself just right.

steps.title: Sweat lab
steps.do: Your child dips one hand in a bowl of warm water, takes it out, and holds both hands in front of a fan (or you wave a newspaper). Ask: 'Which hand feels cooler?' (the wet one). Say: 'When you get hot, your skin makes sweat. As the sweat dries in the air, it carries heat away and cools you. When you are cold, your muscles shiver to make heat and the little hairs on your arms stand up. Your body keeps itself just right, not too hot and not too cold. Scientists call this homeostasis.' Ask: 'What does your body do when it needs water?' (You feel thirsty, and you pass less urine.)

steps.title: Me, made of cells
steps.do: Do the journal page 'Me, made of cells'. On one half of a page your child draws themselves, whole. On the other half they draw a big circle as if looking through a microscope, and fill it with tiny shapes: round blood cells, long muscle cells, star-shaped nerve cells, and little rod-shaped microbes. Say: 'Your one body is made of about 30 trillion tiny living cells, each one alive. And living on you and inside your tummy are about as many microbes again, tiny living things that help you digest food. You are one person, made of a crowd of living cells working together.' Ask: 'If many of your cells are always being replaced, are you still the same you as last year?' Listen; there is no right answer.

steps.title: Puppet dance and body yoga
steps.do: Play music. You are the puppeteer: pretend to pull a string tied to one joint (elbow, knee, wrist, shoulder, hip) and your child moves only that joint, stiffly, like Ponni. Then say 'Your strings are inside now!' and they dance freely, using every joint. End with three yoga poses held for five slow breaths each: mountain (stand tall, feel the spine stretch up), tree (stand on one foot, the other foot on the inside of the leg, hands together: feel the ankle muscles keep you balanced) and child's pose (kneel and fold forward: feel the back bones round). Ask: 'Which pose made which muscles work?'

need: a bowl of warm water, a fan or newspaper

days.title: Teach it back
days.goal: Review the whole rung, try the challenge puzzles and teach it back.

steps.title: Picture tour
steps.do: Bring out the life-size picture from Day 1. Ask your child to add three things they now know are inside: draw the skull in the head, the ribs in the chest and a line of beads for the spine. Mark the joints with red dots. Ask: 'Which part was hardest to live without this week, the thumb or the elbow?'

steps.title: Big questions
steps.do: Ask one big question and really listen: 'A puppet needs someone to pull its strings. Who pulls yours?' Then the challenge question: 'Is a skeleton something dead and spooky?' (No: your bones are alive and growing right now; they have blood in them and mend when they break.)

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child is the teacher. They teach a grown-up or a toy: the names of ten parts, one joint and how it moves, how a muscle pulls, and why a thumb is special. Then ask the check questions. If they want more, do Worksheet ws3 together.

opts: only when you are a baby

sections.p: What if your skeleton were made of jelly? What could you not do?
A puppet needs a puppeteer. A robot needs a battery. What does your body need to move? Think of three things.
Draw your arm with the bone inside it and the muscle that pulls it up.

experiments.title: A morning without thumbs
experiments.question: What does the thumb do for us?
need: soft cloth tape or soft hair bands
a water bottle with a screw lid
steps: Gently tape or tie each thumb flat against the side of the hand. Not tight.
Try five jobs: do up a button, pick up five rice grains, write your name, open the bottle, tear and eat a piece of dosa or chapati.
Mark each job: tick (easy), wavy line (hard), cross (impossible).
Take the tape off and do the same jobs again. Notice how the thumb moves.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which job do you think will be impossible without thumbs?'
experiments.observe: Which jobs became hard or impossible, and how the child tried to manage (using two hands, using teeth, giving up).
experiments.why: The human thumb can turn and press against the tips of all the other fingers. Scientists call this an opposable thumb. It lets us pinch tiny things and grip tools firmly. Monkeys and apes have thumbs that can do some of this, but ours is longer and stronger compared with our fingers, which is part of why we can hold a pencil so finely.
experiments.safety: Use soft tape, never tight, and take it off at once if your child's hand feels tingly or hurts. A grown-up opens anything hot or sharp.

experiments.title: The stiff elbow
experiments.question: What does a joint let us do?
steps: Roll a newspaper into a tube big enough to slide over your child's arm.
Slide it over the elbow and tape it loosely so the arm stays straight.
Ask your child to pick up a biscuit and eat it with that hand.
Then try touching the top of the head, and scratching the nose.
Take the tube off and do it again.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will you be able to eat the biscuit with a straight arm?'
experiments.observe: Which jobs needed the elbow to bend, and the clever tricks your child used instead.
experiments.why: The elbow is a hinge joint where the upper arm bone meets the two bones of the lower arm. A muscle at the front of the upper arm pulls the lower arm up, folding the arm at the joint. Without that bend, the hand cannot reach the mouth. Every joint lets the skeleton move in its own way: a hinge goes one way, a ball joint goes round.
experiments.safety: Keep the tube loose and take it off after a few minutes.

experiments.title: Foot and forearm
experiments.question: Are some parts of our body the same length as others?
need: a piece of string or wool
steps: Measure your child's foot from heel to big toe with string and cut it.
Hold the string along the inside of the forearm, from the wrist crease to the elbow crease.
Do the same for every person at home.
Compare: is the foot string about the same as the forearm?
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Is your foot longer, shorter or the same as your arm from wrist to elbow?'
experiments.observe: In most people the two are close to the same. Note who is different.
experiments.why: Human bodies grow in a pattern, so some lengths come out roughly matched, like foot and forearm, or arm span and height. They are never exactly the same, and every person is a little different. Bodies are alike in plan and different in detail.

activities.title: Life-size me
need: a big sheet of paper or newspapers taped together
steps: Your child lies on the paper with arms and legs a little apart.
Draw round them with a crayon.
Your child colours in the face and clothes.
Write and stick labels with arrows for 18 body parts.
Keep it on the wall: you will add bones and joints later.
activities.outcome: A life-size labelled picture of your child, which grows during the week as bones, joints and care rules are added.

activities.title: The card arm
need: two strips of card about 15 cm by 3 cm
a piece of string 30 cm long
steps: Cut two strips of card: one is the upper arm, one the lower arm.
Overlap their ends and push a split pin through to make the elbow.
Tape one end of the string to the lower arm, about 2 cm past the elbow.
Make a small tape loop on the upper arm near the shoulder end and thread the string through it.
Hold the upper arm still and pull the string: the lower arm lifts.
activities.outcome: A model arm that bends when the 'muscle' string pulls, showing bone, joint and muscle working together.

project.title: My body book
steps: Draw round your hand and label the thumb and every finger joint.
Draw your skeleton inside the outline of your body, using the life-size picture as a guide.
Add a page of 'things my body did today' (ran, jumped, held a pencil, smelled food).
Add a page of 'my body is different because…' and 'my body is the same because…'.
Show the book to someone at home and explain one page.
project.outcome: A small book of four pages about your child's own body, inside and out.

game.title: Bone Builder
rules: Do what the square says. If you cannot, move back one square.
If you land on a question square and answer well, move forward one more.
The first to reach DANCE wins, and everyone does a dance using as many joints as they can.
squares: Touch your elbow to your knee: +1
Name two bones you can feel
Name a job that is hard without a thumb
Bend your hip and your knee: which is the hinge?
Pull like a muscle: flex your arm
Spin your shoulder round: it is a ball joint! +2
Fell off the wall: back 2 and wear a helmet next time
Count your pairs: eyes, ears, hands…
Feel your ribs: what do they guard?
Sat still all day: miss a turn
Name a body part a bird and you both have

big: About half the living cells in and on your body are microbes, not human cells. Are the microbes part of you?
A puppet needs someone to pull its strings. Who pulls yours?
Your bones are inside you all the time, but you have never seen them. How do you know they are there?
A bird, a bat, a whale and you all have the same bones in your arms. Why would that be?
Is a person with one hand, or who uses a wheelchair, any less a human body?
What is the most important part of your body? Can you choose just one?

challenge.q: People say skeletons are dead, spooky things.
challenge.hint: The skeleton in your body is alive. Bones have blood flowing through them, they grow, they get stronger when you run and jump, and they mend themselves when they break. A skeleton only looks dead after a body has died. Ask: what in your body is not alive?

challenge.q: People say grown-ups have more of everything than children.
challenge.hint: A newborn baby has about 300 bones and soft pieces that will become bone. As the child grows, many of them join together, so a grown-up has 206. Ask: where do you think some of your bones will join? (The skull starts as several pieces with soft gaps that close.)

challenge.q: A book says it, so it must be true.
challenge.hint: For over a thousand years doctors in Europe trusted the books of Galen, a Greek doctor, about the body. Andreas Vesalius looked at real human bodies and found Galen had made mistakes because he had studied monkeys and other animals. Ask: how can you check a book?

perspectives.who: A bommalattam puppeteer from Tamil Nadu
perspectives.view: Puppeteers know that a puppet only looks alive if its strings are tied at the right places: at the joints. A puppet with no joints cannot dance. Ask: where would you tie the strings on a puppet of yourself?

perspectives.who: A child who was born without one hand
perspectives.view: Many children born without a hand learn to do almost everything, using the other hand, the arm, the chin and feet in clever ways. Ask: what does that tell you about how bodies and brains learn?
A bat's wing is their hand: long finger bones with skin stretched between them. Ask: how is a bat's hand like yours, and how is it different?

voices.who: Sushruta and the Sushruta Samhita, ancient India (historians date the text to between about the 6th century BCE and the early centuries CE)
voices.idea: The Sushruta Samhita, a Sanskrit book of surgery named after the teacher Sushruta, says that a surgeon must not rely only on books but must learn the body by looking carefully inside it, layer by layer. It counts about 300 bones.
voices.then: The book was studied and copied in India for centuries and later translated into Arabic.
voices.now: Historians agree the text teaches careful observation of the body. Its count of about 300 differs from today's 206 for an adult mainly because it counted things we now call cartilage, teeth and nails. The exact dates of the text and how much was added later are still debated.
voices.ask: If you and a friend counted the bones in your hand, how could you make sure you both counted the same things?

voices.who: Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564), Belgium and Italy, and the artists who drew his book
voices.idea: In 1543 Vesalius published a huge book about the human body, 'De humani corporis fabrica' (On the Fabric of the Human Body). He had looked inside human bodies himself and showed that the famous Greek doctor Galen had made mistakes, because Galen had mostly studied animals such as monkeys.
voices.then: Some doctors were angry: Galen had been trusted for about 1,300 years. Vesalius's own teacher Jacobus Sylvius attacked him.
voices.now: Vesalius was right, and his book changed medicine. Its wonderful drawings were made by artists, probably from the workshop of the painter Titian; one may have been Jan van Calcar. Their names are not on the pictures, so we cannot be sure who drew them.
voices.ask: The drawings made the book famous, but we don't know for sure who drew them. Should the artist's name be on the book too?

books.title: From Head to Toe
books.author: Eric Carle
books.why: Animals show off their body parts, and the child copies each move: a happy way to name parts and joints.

books.title: Funnybones
books.author: Janet and Allan Ahlberg
books.why: A gentle, funny story of skeletons who fall apart and put themselves back together, good for naming bones.

books.title: The Skeleton Inside You
books.author: Philip Balestrino
books.why: A clear, simple first science book about what bones do and how they grow.

books.title: Here Are My Hands
books.author: Bill Martin Jr and John Archambault
books.why: A rhyming book about what each body part is for, with children of many backgrounds.

check.q: Show me your wrist, ankle, hip, elbow and heel.
Name three parts you have two of.
check.a: Any three of: eyes, ears, hands, arms, legs, feet, knees, elbows, nostrils.
A place where two bones meet so the body can bend, like a knee or elbow.
They pull on bones to move them. They can only pull, not push.
It can touch every other finger, so we can pinch, grip and hold a pencil.

check.q: Does a baby have more bones or fewer than a grown-up?
check.a: More, about 300. Many join together as the child grows, leaving 206.

check.q: How does your body cool down when you are hot?
check.a: It sweats. As the sweat dries, it carries heat away. When you are cold, you shiver.

check.q: What does a bird's wing have inside it that is like your arm?
check.a: The same kinds of bones: one upper arm bone, two lower arm bones and hand bones.

story.title: Ponni and the Strings Inside
text: I am Ponni. I am a bommalattam puppet, a string puppet from Tamil Nadu, and I was carved from wood in a village near Kumbakonam forty years ago. My face is painted pink and white, my eyes are big and black, and my skirt is red with tiny mirrors sewn into it, so that when I spin, I flash like a fistful of stars.

I cannot spin by myself. I want you to know that at the start. I have a wooden head, a wooden body and soft cloth arms, and at my wrists and my waist and the top of my head there are black strings. The strings go up, up, into the hands of Kamala, who has worked me since she was a girl. When she moves a finger, I dance. When she sleeps, I lie in the tin box with the other puppets, the king and the demon and the horse, and I do not move at all.
For forty years this did not trouble me. Then Kavya was born.

Kavya is Kamala's granddaughter. When she was very small, she lay on a mat beside the puppet stage at the temple festival and waved her arms and kicked her legs while I danced. I watched her through the gap in the curtain. Nobody was pulling her strings. Her arms went up, all by themselves. Her legs went round, all by themselves. How?

I looked very hard for her strings. I looked above her head. Nothing. I looked at the ceiling of the tent. Nothing. I decided that perhaps her strings were invisible, very thin, like the threads a spider lets down from a roof.

Kavya grew. She learned to sit, and stand, and walk, and then, one winter, she learned to dance. She danced beside the stage while I danced on it, and she copied me. When I lifted my arms, she lifted hers. When I spun, she spun, and the mirrors on her own small skirt flashed too.

And I noticed something. When she bent her knee, it bent in one place only, in the middle of her leg. My knee bends in the middle of my leg too, at the place where Kamala's father carved two pieces of wood and joined them with a little peg. When she bent her elbow, it bent in one place only. So does mine. Her wrist turned. So does mine. Where she bent, I bent.
So you are a puppet too, I thought. A puppet with pegs inside you. But where, where were her strings?
One evening, after the show, Kavya sat on the tin box with her grandmother, swinging her legs. Paati was rubbing her hands, which had grown old and stiff.
“Paati,” she said, “who pulls my strings?”
Paati laughed. “Put your hand here,” she said, and she laid Kavya's left hand flat on the front of Kavya's right arm, above the elbow. “Now lift your hand up to your shoulder. Slowly.”
Kavya lifted it. Her eyes went wide.
“It's going fat!” she said. “Something under my skin is going fat and hard!”

“That is your muscle,” said her grandmother. “And under it, feel, there is something hard that does not change. That is your bone. The bone is like Ponni's wood. The place where it bends is like Ponni's peg. And the muscle is your string. It is tied to the bone, inside you, and when it pulls, the bone moves.”
“So I have strings,” said Kavya slowly. “Inside.”
“Hundreds,” said Paati. “Strings for your fingers and your toes and your eyes and your tongue. More strings than any puppet in Tamil Nadu.”
“And who pulls them?”
Her grandmother tapped her gently on the forehead. “You do.”

From the tin box, I heard all of this. I lay very still, as I always do, and I thought about it all night. Her strings were inside her. Mine were outside me. That was the whole difference. She was wood and pegs and strings, like me, only soft and warm, and the hand that pulled her strings was her own.
I was jealous, a little. Then I was not.
Because the next year, at the temple festival, Paati's hands hurt too much to work my strings. She sat on a stool and sighed. The crowd was waiting. The drum was ready.

Kavya climbed onto the stool beside her. She took my strings in her two small hands. I felt it at once: a new hand, lighter, a little shaky. Her fingers bent at their little joints. The muscles in her arms pulled her bones, and her hands pulled my strings, and my strings lifted my arms.
And I danced. I spun, and my mirrors flashed like a fistful of stars, and the crowd clapped, and Paati on her stool clapped loudest of all.
Her strings pulled my strings. That is how it is now. I do not dance by myself, and I find I do not mind. Nobody, it turns out, dances completely by themselves.
story.epiphany: We move because muscles inside us pull on bones, and the bones bend at joints: the body is like a puppet whose strings are inside and pulled by itself. The turn comes when Kavya feels her own muscle go fat and hard over the bone and her grandmother says 'You do'. Underneath, gently: Ponni, Kavya and her grandmother move one another, so no one dances entirely alone.
ask: How were Ponni and Kavya the same? How were they different?
What did Kavya feel when she lifted her hand to her shoulder?
What are Kavya's 'strings' really, and where are her 'pegs'?
At the end, whose strings pulled whose?
Ponni says nobody dances completely by themselves. What do you think she means?

ideas.idea: Your muscles pull your bones, and you control them.
ideas.more: Bones are the frame, joints are the bends and muscles are the strings that pull. Your brain sends the message to pull. Feel it every time you bend your arm.
They grow, they have blood in them and they mend when broken. A baby has about 300 bones and pieces that join into 206.

ideas.idea: Your body is made of trillions of living cells.
ideas.more: One you, made of about 30 trillion living cells, with about as many microbes living on and in you (the best count today, from 2016, says roughly one microbe for every human cell). All of them work together, and your body keeps itself 'just right' by sweating, shivering and feeling thirsty.

ideas.idea: Many animals with backbones have the same arm bones as you.
ideas.more: A bird's wing, a whale's flipper, a bat's wing and your arm have the same bones, shaped for different jobs. We are related to them all.

unknowns: Why did the human thumb become so long and strong? Scientists argue about whether it was for making tools, throwing, or something else; nobody knows for sure.
How does your brain know exactly where your arm is, even with your eyes shut? Scientists understand part of it but are still finding out how all the signals are put together.
